limitations: The rule text supplies no definition of how randomized facts are initially established or propagated outside this specification.
The order expression excludes use before Ins and only recognizes the exact event set named in the rule.
The two-argument g2 event does not cover three-argument getInstance overloads present in modern Java APIs.
No AspectJ target(...) or args(...) pointcut appears in this CrySL rule; subtype matching semantics cannot be inferred from this rule text.
predicates: randomized[seed] is required before SecureRandom(byte[]) and setSeed(byte[]).
randomized[this] is ensured after any Ins event.
randomized[genSeed], randomized[bytes], randomized[randInt], and randomized[randIntInRange] are ensured after their respective End events.
algorithm must be one of SHA1PRNG, Windows-PRNG, NativePRNG, NativePRNGBlocking, NativePRNGNonBlocking, or PKCS11 for g1 and g2.
detector_semantics.claim: The CrySL rule declares randomized[this] after an Ins event, randomized[genSeed] after generateSeed, randomized[bytes] after nextBytes, randomized[randInt] after nextInt(), and randomized[randIntInRange] after nextInt(int). It requires randomized[seed] for SecureRandom(byte[]) and setSeed(byte[]), and randomized[lSeed] for setSeed(long).

unknowns: The supplied CrySL rule does not define the operational semantics, trusted sources, or propagation rules for randomized[...].

The supplied CrySL rule does not state whether the detector models dynamic dispatch to subclasses of java.security.SecureRandom, nor how it handles Kotlin aliases, reflection, generated bytecode, or native calls.
The rule does not explain why its algorithm allow-list is limited to six names or whether that list is intended to be portable across Java versions and providers.
The rule does not cover newer SecureRandom overloads and APIs, including parameterized getInstance overloads with three arguments, parameterized nextBytes, and reseed.
The rule does not specify whether a discarded generateSeed or nextInt result should still be treated as a meaningful randomized value for downstream analysis.
The rule does not establish a relationship between its randomized predicate and any particular cryptographic use requirement, entropy estimate, compliance regime, or threat model.

documented_behavior: java.security.SecureRandom is documented by Oracle as a cryptographically strong random number generator; the API documentation states that seed material supplied to it must be unpredictable and that output sequences must be cryptographically strong.
The no-argument constructor selects a default SecureRandom implementation. The byte[] constructor creates a default implementation and seeds it with the supplied bytes.

getInstance(String) and its provider/parameter overloads return a SecureRandom for a requested RNG algorithm; getInstanceStrong() selects from the runtime securerandom.strongAlgorithms security property.

setSeed(byte[]) and setSeed(long) supplement rather than replace existing seed material. The documentation warns that calling setSeed before a PRNG has self-seeded prevents automatic self-seeding, and that the caller must supply enough entropy.

generateSeed(int) returns a requested number of seed bytes; nextBytes(byte[]) fills the supplied array; inherited nextInt() returns an int and nextInt(int) returns a value from zero inclusive to the bound exclusive.
preconditions: SecureRandom(byte[]) and setSeed(byte[]) reject null byte arrays.
getInstance methods require a non-null algorithm and can fail when no suitable provider or algorithm is available.
generateSeed(int) rejects a negative byte count.
The inherited nextInt(int) requires a positive bound.
The detector rule additionally requires its static randomized predicate for byte[] and long explicit seed inputs.
unknowns: Which provider and implementation are selected by the no-argument constructor or provider-unspecified getInstance calls is runtime configuration dependent.
Whether each algorithm name in the rule is recognized or installed is Java version, provider, operating-system, and security-configuration dependent.
The API documentation does not map the CrySL randomized predicate to a quantitative entropy threshold or a concrete provenance test.

events.condition: Observed when overload resolution selects java.security.SecureRandom() with zero arguments. The rule has no input predicate for this event; after Ins it ensures randomized[this].
events.name: c1

events.condition: Observed only when overload resolution selects the one-argument java.security.SecureRandom(byte[]) constructor. The argument value bound as seed must satisfy randomized[seed] before the call; source spelling or a variable name alone does not satisfy that predicate. After Ins the rule ensures randomized[this].
events.name: c2

events.condition: Observed only for the one-argument getInstance(String) overload. The value bound as algorithm must be exactly one of SHA1PRNG, Windows-PRNG, NativePRNG, NativePRNGBlocking, NativePRNGNonBlocking, or PKCS11. A literal is only one way to establish that value constraint. After Ins the rule ensures randomized[this].
events.name: g1

events.condition: Observed only for a two-argument getInstance(algorithm, _) call, as written in the CrySL rule. The algorithm value must be exactly one of SHA1PRNG, Windows-PRNG, NativePRNG, NativePRNGBlocking, NativePRNGNonBlocking, or PKCS11; the second argument is unconstrained by this rule. After Ins the rule ensures randomized[this].
events.name: g2

events.condition: Observed for the zero-argument getInstanceStrong() factory. The rule attaches no algorithm-string constraint to this event. After Ins the rule ensures randomized[this].
events.name: gI

events.condition: Observed only when overload resolution selects java.security.SecureRandom.setSeed(byte[]). The byte-array argument bound as seed must already satisfy randomized[seed]. This is a rule predicate, not an assertion that the source visibly contains a random-producing expression.
events.name: s1

events.condition: Observed only when overload resolution selects java.security.SecureRandom.setSeed(long). The long argument bound as lSeed must already satisfy randomized[lSeed]. This is a rule predicate, not a runtime test written into the application.
events.name: s2

events.condition: Observed for java.security.SecureRandom.generateSeed(int). The returned byte[] value bound as genSeed obtains randomized[genSeed] after the call; the CrySL event has no additional input predicate.
events.name: gS

events.condition: Observed for java.security.SecureRandom.nextBytes(byte[]). The supplied byte[] value bound as bytes obtains randomized[bytes] after the call; the CrySL event has no additional input predicate.
events.name: nB

events.condition: Observed for the inherited zero-argument nextInt() call on a java.security.SecureRandom receiver. The returned int bound as randInt obtains randomized[randInt] after the call.
events.name: nI

events.condition: Observed for the inherited one-int-argument nextInt(int) call on a java.security.SecureRandom receiver. The returned int bound as randIntInRange obtains randomized[randIntInRange] after the call. The rule imposes no predicate on range.
events.name: nIR

important_note: This is a CrySL static protocol and predicate specification for java.security.SecureRandom. It tracks a narrow set of construction, factory, seeding, and output calls; it does not by itself measure entropy, verify a provider implementation, prove that execution reaches a cryptographic sink, or establish the real-world unpredictability of a particular runtime value.
forbidden_inferences_without_evidence: An unmet randomized[seed] or randomized[lSeed] requirement does not prove that the runtime seed is predictable or attacker-controlled.
A satisfied randomized predicate does not prove a specific entropy quantity, independence, freshness, secrecy, or suitability for a particular protocol.
A permitted algorithm string does not prove that the algorithm is available from the installed providers, that the selected provider is the intended provider, or that the call succeeds.
Creation through getInstanceStrong() does not identify the actual selected algorithm or provider; those are determined from runtime security configuration.
The rule does not establish that generated values are later used as keys, nonces, tokens, salts, identifiers, or any other security-sensitive artifact.
The rule does not cover every SecureRandom API overload or every random-producing inherited method.
The CrySL source alone does not define the analyzer's precise interprocedural, aliasing, subclass-dispatch, reflection, native-code, or Kotlin-lowering behavior.

security_semantics.runtime_claim: At successful runtime execution, SecureRandom APIs have the behavior documented by the installed Java implementation and selected provider. The Java API contract describes SecureRandom as cryptographically strong and requires caller-supplied seed material to be unpredictable, but runtime strength still depends on provider implementation, provider selection, system entropy sources, configuration, and successful calls.
security_semantics.detector_claim: The detector claims only that a required CrySL randomized fact is present for explicit seed inputs, that the event sequence conforms to the listed protocol, that listed factory algorithm values satisfy the fixed allow-list, and that listed outputs obtain the rule's randomized fact.

compatibility: Check that the deployment JDK and installed providers recognize the requested algorithm and overload.
Check whether provider-specific names such as NativePRNG, NativePRNGBlocking, NativePRNGNonBlocking, Windows-PRNG, or PKCS11 are available in the target environment.
Check modern API use separately: the rule does not list getInstance overloads with three arguments, nextBytes(byte[], SecureRandomParameters), reseed, or other inherited random-output APIs.
runtime: To evaluate actual runtime strength, record the selected provider, SecureRandom algorithm, Java runtime version, relevant security properties, and whether calls complete successfully.
For explicit seed material, obtain evidence of its runtime provenance, unpredictability, amount of entropy, freshness, and attacker influence.
If getInstanceStrong() is used, inspect the effective securerandom.strongAlgorithms configuration and the provider and algorithm actually selected.
source_level: Resolve the receiver and selected overload to java.security.SecureRandom.

For a reported seed requirement, identify whether the call is SecureRandom(byte[]), setSeed(byte[]), or setSeed(long), and trace the corresponding argument value to evidence sufficient for the detector's randomized predicate.
For a reported getInstance algorithm constraint, establish the value of the algorithm argument rather than relying only on the spelling of its variable.
Check the event order against Ins, (Seed?, End*)*.

name: SecureRandomSpec
semantic_scope: For every finding of this rule, the detector models the lifecycle of a java.security.SecureRandom instance: creation through two constructors or three listed factories, optional seeding, and selected byte/int/seed output operations. It enforces a fixed algorithm allow-list for the listed getInstance calls, requires a pre-established randomized predicate for explicit byte[] or long seed material, and propagates its randomized predicate to the instance and to values produced by the listed output operations.
known_false_positive_shapes: A byte[] or long is genuinely supplied from a strong runtime entropy source, but the detector cannot derive its randomized predicate through the available source, library, native, reflection, serialization, or interprocedural path.

A deterministic setSeed call occurs only after a SecureRandom PRNG has already self-seeded. Oracle documents that setSeed supplements existing seed material and repeated calls do not reduce randomness, while the rule nevertheless requires randomized input for every modeled setSeed call.

The code uses an algorithm accepted and securely implemented by the target provider but not contained in the rule's fixed six-name allow-list, such as a modern provider-supported algorithm outside that list.

A source-level pattern resembles a listed method call but overload resolution or receiver typing differs from java.security.SecureRandom; local substring matching without type resolution would be insufficient.
protocol: Ins, (Seed?, End*)*; Ins = SecureRandom() | SecureRandom(byte[]) | getInstance(String) | getInstance(String, _) | getInstanceStrong(); Seed = setSeed(byte[]) | setSeed(long); End = generateSeed(int) | nextBytes(byte[]) | nextInt() | nextInt(int).

detector_examples.message: the constructor expects a byte array observed to come from a randomized source
